edits.before: So the rating and the withdrawal come apart, and only one of them is shared. And that disclosure measure is the most useful number in the week: how much a person opens up is not a fixed property of that person. It moves with who they are sitting opposite. Week 9 met the same claim from an entirely different literature, when Kluger and Malloy argued that a large share of the variance in question-asking belongs to the particular pair rather than the person. Two methods, two fields, one shape — which is the best reason this course has to prefer interoperation to conversion.
edits.after: Week 11 distinguishes an unfavourable rating from a decision not to meet again. It also uses the disclosure result to ask what changes with the partner. Week 9 raises a related question through Kluger and Malloy's argument that much of the variance in question-asking belongs to the particular pair rather than the person.
edits.reason: Keep the two useful connections without collapsing different studies into a triumphant single argument.
